title: He descended (CCC 632–637)
hook: he went to the dead to open heaven for the just who went before

segments.voice: Yesterday, under Pontius Pilate: a real governor, and a death charged to no single people. Your line was we all share it. Did you catch a they all sentence and let it go? Day one thousand seventy-seven.

Friday evening, the body is laid in a tomb and a stone is rolled across the door. The women go home and, as Luke puts it, rest on the sabbath according to the commandment. Then Sunday morning, the empty tomb. In between, the Gospels say almost nothing. Catholic churches keep Holy Saturday bare and quiet. And yet the Apostles' Creed has a line for exactly that silence. Between buried and rose again, it says: he descended into hell. It is a strange line to say out loud, and today's word is the beginning of it.
screen: `FRIDAY: THE STONE.` → `SATURDAY: SILENCE.` → `HE DESCENDED INTO HELL.`

segments.voice: First, what hell means in that line. The Catechism says scripture calls the place of the dead hell: Sheol in Hebrew, Hades in Greek. It's the realm of those who died before Christ, deprived of the sight of God, the just and the wicked alike, all waiting. So the line is not saying Jesus went to the place of the damned. The Catechism is precise about this. He did not go down to free the damned, or to destroy the hell of damnation. He went to free the just who had gone before him. Second, what it says about his death. When the New Testament says Jesus was raised from the dead, the Catechism notes, it means he had truly been among the dead. He died as people die, and went where the dead go. Third, what he did there. The first letter of Peter says that Christ, in the Douay-Rheims, "preached to those spirits that were in prison." And a little later the same letter says the gospel was preached even to the dead. The Catechism calls this the last phase of his mission: the good news reaching people of every time and place, all the way back. Then it quotes what it calls an ancient homily for Holy Saturday. In it, Christ goes down looking for Adam, the first man, like a shepherd looking for a lost sheep, takes him by the hand, and tells him to rise. Some icons of the resurrection paint that very moment: Christ standing on broken gates, pulling Adam and Eve up out of their tombs. Holy Saturday looks silent from above. In Catholic teaching, down below it was loud.
screen: `HELL HERE MEANS THE PLACE OF THE DEAD.` · `HE TRULY DIED.` · `PREACHED TO THE SPIRITS IN PRISON.` · `CHRIST GOES LOOKING FOR ADAM.` · then, large: `EVEN THE DEAD HEARD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember your ancestors. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind those who came before you: a grandparent, a great-grandmother whose name you only half know, the people further back whose names nobody kept. Say the names you have, quietly, one by one. For the ones without names, let a place or a language or a recipe stand in for them. If you pray, you can pray for them, as Catholics pray for the dead. If you don't, simply hold one thing of theirs you still carry. The bell holds the time.
He descended. The Creed's line for Holy Saturday: Christ truly died and went among the dead, to free the just who had gone before him. Today's word.
Your line: even the dead heard. Today, tell someone one story about an ancestor, or ask an older relative for one you don't know yet. Day one thousand seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics profess Christ's descent to the dead in the Apostles' Creed, keep Holy Saturday as a quiet day of waiting at the tomb, and pray for the dead, above all at Mass and in November.

notes: Confirm Challoner wording of 1 Peter 3:19 ('In which also coming he preached to those spirits that were in prison').
CCC 632 (truly among the dead), 633 (Sheol/Hades; not to free the damned but the just), 634 (last phase of the messianic mission), 635 (Holy Saturday homily) paraphrased.
'There's no Mass during the day' on Holy Saturday: liturgical norm (no Mass until the Easter Vigil). Confirm phrasing.

'Some icons of the resurrection paint that very moment' (the Anastasis icon): a general claim about iconography not stated in the day's cited texts. Keeper may soften to 'some icons' or cut; it also drives the fork.
'Down below it was loud' is an image, not a doctrine; Keeper may cut.
Creed line 'he descended into hell' given in the traditional English wording without quotation marks.
